title: King Lear
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — A Room of State in King Lear’s Palace
about:
Lear plans to give away his kingdom and keep a hundred knights. With the court watching, he asks his three daughters which of them loves him most. Goneril and Regan oblige. Cordelia, his favorite, says she loves him as a daughter should. Lear gives her share to her sisters and banishes Kent for objecting. The King of France marries Cordelia without a dowry.

Gloucester also mistakes which child he can trust. His son Edmund uses a forged letter to turn him against Edgar, his heir. Edgar escapes by taking on the voice and rags of a wandering beggar. When Lear loses his shelter and Gloucester loses his sight, both fathers find themselves depending on people they once barely noticed.

Two early printed versions survive, the 1608 Quarto and the 1623 Folio. This edition combines readings from both. It includes Lear’s mock trial of his daughters and gives the play’s last speech to Edgar.

angleCards.title: The love test
angleCards.text: The whole play begins with one decision: Lear stages a public competition to see which daughter loves him most. Watch what that decision says about him, and what each daughter actually does with it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read King Lear as a study of what Lear's love test asks for, what each daughter does in response, and what the play thinks of a man who needs love to be performed.

angleCards.title: Madness on the heath
angleCards.text: Caught in the storm, Lear notices his Fool shivering. Soon he is asking how anyone without a roof survives such a night. Listen to how the object of his concern changes.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the storm scenes on the heath — Lear's collapse into madness, the Fool, the disguised Edgar — as the play's moral and philosophical centre.

angleCards.title: Fathers and children
angleCards.text: Lear has three daughters. Gloucester has two sons. Both fathers are betrayed by the children they trusted and helped by the ones they cast off. The two plots mirror each other deliberately.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Lear and Gloucester plots together as parallel studies of fathers misreading their children, and decide what the play makes of the symmetry.

angleCards.title: The ending
angleCards.text: Cordelia and Lear find each other again. In prison he imagines the two of them telling stories and singing. Listen to what becomes of that future in the last scene.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read King Lear with attention to its ending — Shakespeare's decision to kill Cordelia — and to what difference that single change makes to the meaning of the play.

cast.name: King Lear
cast.description: Lear says he is over eighty. He gives away the land and the power to govern but expects to keep his title, his knights and his daughters’ obedience. Out in the storm, even finding shelter for the Fool becomes a question he has to answer himself.

cast.name: Cordelia
cast.description: Lear’s youngest daughter answers her father plainly and leaves without a dowry as Queen of France. At Dover she sends soldiers to find him and asks a physician how to help him recover.

cast.name: Goneril and Regan
cast.description: Goneril is married to Albany, Regan to Cornwall. Each receives part of Lear’s kingdom. They dispute the size of his retinue and eventually compete for Edmund. Listen for the moments when cooperation gives way to suspicion.

cast.name: The Earl of Gloucester
cast.description: Gloucester has two sons, Edgar, his heir, and Edmund, born outside marriage. Edmund tricks him into driving Edgar away. Later Gloucester risks his life to find Lear shelter.

cast.name: Edmund
cast.description: Edmund resents the law that makes his brother the heir. His forged letter turns father against son. Listen for the difference between the voice he uses when alone and the concern he performs for his family.

cast.name: Edgar
cast.description: Driven into hiding, Edgar plays Poor Tom, a nearly naked beggar tormented by spirits. He must keep changing his voice to guide his blinded father without revealing his name. This edition gives him the closing lines, as the Folio does.

acclaim.quote: if it can sustain this comparison, may be judged to be the most perfect specimen of the dramatic art existing in the world
acclaim.context: A Defence of Poetry, written in 1821, published in 1840. Excerpt from a comparison with Greek tragedy.

acclaim.quote: It is then the best of all Shakespear’s plays, for it is the one in which he was the most in earnest.

whyItMatters.title: Two endings to the reunion
whyItMatters.body: The older play King Leir restores the father to his throne. Shakespeare lets father and daughter meet again, then asks the audience to watch Lear carry Cordelia’s body onstage. Watch what happens to his hope: first a mirror might catch her breath, then a feather seems to move, then he asks the others to look at her lips.

whyItMatters.title: Who has a roof?
whyItMatters.body: Out on the heath, Lear first fights the wind as though it could take orders. At the hovel he notices that the Fool is cold. He begins to picture people who always live without shelter and to ask what he did for them when he was king. Edgar, disguised as Poor Tom, comes out of the straw before Lear has finished reckoning with that question.

whyItMatters.title: Two fathers who fail to recognize their children
whyItMatters.body: Lear has heard Cordelia speak the truth and punishes her for it. Gloucester sees what looks like Edgar’s handwriting and scarcely needs another reason to condemn him. Much later one father recognizes his daughter’s voice and another takes his own son’s arm without knowing who is guiding him. Follow the different paths by which they come to trust their children.
